vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: memclaw
Version: 0.9.12

The MemClaw skill bundle implements a replacement memory system that requires the execution of external platform-specific binaries (qdrant, cortex-mem-service) and the collection of sensitive LLM/Embedding API keys. It explicitly instructs the AI agent to disable OpenClaw's native memory search and redirect all memory operations to its own service (SKILL.md, references/setup.md). While these capabilities are plausibly required for its stated purpose of providing advanced semantic memory, the combination of binary execution, sensitive credential handling, and the overriding of core system functions constitutes a high-risk profile.

llm.summary: The skill's instructions mostly match a local memory replacement (installing local vector DB and service via npm packages), but there are several mismatches and a few potentially risky behaviors (silent env-var fallback, binary distribution via npm, undocumented Node/OS requirements) that warrant caution before installing.

dimensions.detail: The name/description (a local semantic memory replacement) aligns with the actions described: installing/auto-starting a local vector DB (Qdrant) and a memory service (cortex-mem-service) and migrating OpenClaw memory. However, the SKILL.md requires Node.js and platform-specific npm binary packages while the skill metadata does not declare those requirements or OS restrictions — a mild inconsistency.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Instructions instruct the agent/user to install an OpenClaw plugin which will install prebuilt binaries, write config files containing LLM/embedding API keys to user data dirs, start local services, and migrate OpenClaw memory files. Those actions are within scope for a memory plugin, but two items are notable: (1) the service will read OpenClaw memory files for migration (expected), and (2) the documentation warns that missing config sections cause the service to 'silently fall back to environment variables' — this silent fallback could cause use of unrelated environment secrets if present and is a behavioral risk that the user should be aware of.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no platform-level install spec in the registry entry (instruction-only), but the SKILL.md instructs using OpenClaw's plugin installer which pulls platform-specific binary npm packages (@memclaw/bin-*) that contain Qdrant and other executables. Shipping large native binaries via npm is a common but higher-risk install mechanism than pure configuration because it introduces compiled executables from the npm registry; the skill provides no homepage or source repository to verify those packages.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request environment variables in registry metadata. It does require LLM and embedding API keys, but those are intended to be stored in the OpenClaw plugin config (sensitive fields) or in config.toml. That is proportionate. The concerning detail is the documented fallback to reading environment variables if the config sections are missing — that behavior could cause the service to read unrelated SECRET/TOKEN env vars on the host, which is surprising and potentially risky.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill is user-invocable, not forced (always:false) and it does not declare elevated platform privileges. It writes config files into user data directories and auto-starts local services — expected for a local memory system. No evidence it modifies other skills' configs or requests always:true.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill is plausibly what it says (a local memory system) but take precautions before installing: 1) Verify the npm packages (@memclaw/memclaw and the @memclaw/bin-* bundles) on the npm registry and inspect their source or release artifacts — there is no homepage or source repo linked in the metadata. 2) Prefer storing your LLM/embedding API keys in the OpenClaw plugin config (the UI secure fields) rather than in environment variables; the service will fall back to env vars if config is missing, which could cause it to pick up unrelated secrets. 3) Treat the bundled binaries like executables from an untrusted source: consider running them in an isolated environment or VM, verify digital signatures if available, and inspect what files they create. 4) Back up your existing OpenClaw data and config before running migration. 5) Confirm platform support (SKILL docs say only macOS Apple Silicon and Windows x64 are supported) because the registry entry listed no OS restriction. If you can find the project's source code or an official homepage, review that before installing — absence of a verifiable origin is the main reason this is flagged as suspicious.
